The only explicit UNC80–autism statements are (i) a review that lists UNC80 among possible susceptibility loci for autism as background rather than primary data (24904279), and (ii) a multigenic 2q34 microdeletion case where the deletion spans UNC80 but MAP2 is favored as the candidate (29632546) — a CNV cannot single out UNC80. The UNC79 report describing a patient with autistic features (37183800) concerns a different gene of the same channelosome, which supports biological plausibility rather than direct UNC80 evidence. Therefore the relationship is best described as hypothesized (shared channelosome biology, neuronal excitability, severe NDD/ID that overlaps ASD risk) with some weight to "Existing" because severe NDD/ID phenotypes and the susceptibility-locus claim could be read as limited human evidence.

justification: ZNF462 haploinsufficiency causes Weiss-Kruszka syndrome, and autism/autistic behaviour is a recurrent component of this neurodevelopmental phenotype in humans. Direct evidence from sequence-level variants in independent probands includes the phenotype delineation cohort of 24 individuals with ZNF462 loss-of-function variants, of whom 33% had autism spectrum disorder (PMID 31361404), and a pedigree study in which a proband with a de novo splice variant (c.6696-2A>C, functionally validated by minigene assay) showed autistic behaviour (PMID 39501256). A de novo translocation disrupting ZNF462 (and KLF12) in a patient with ASD and syndromic ID adds support, though two genes were affected (PMID 29427787). Counterbalancing this, ASD is only a minority, variably penetrant feature of a broader multiple-congenital-anomaly/developmental-delay syndrome rather than an isolated, consistently replicated ASD association, and other reports (PMIDs 28513610, 39287049, 40949918) emphasize dysmorphism and developmental delay without systematic ASD ascertainment. Hence probability is split between Established (syndromic ASD, replicated in human probands) and Existing (limited, partially penetrant evidence).

justification: Coe et al. (PMID 25217958) provide primary evidence: resequencing identified truncating ZMYND11 single-nucleotide variants in multiple individuals with autism, aggression and complex neuropsychiatric features, isolating the gene from the 10p15.3 CNV interval. Independent single-gene (non-CNV) support includes a de novo missense variant with autistic-like phenotype (PMID 27626064) and a de novo pathogenic ZMYND11 variant in a child with infection-provoked autistic regression (PMID 39985218), plus large cohorts of ZMYND11 point-variant carriers with prominent behavioral/neurodevelopmental abnormalities (PMIDs 32097528, 34216016) and ASD reported in gene-defined cohorts (PMID 38844245). Mechanistic work (ZMYND11 as chromatin reader restraining KMT2A; mouse neuronal deletion causing dendritic and behavioral abnormalities, PMID 41279818) and iPSC models give biological plausibility but are not human genetic evidence. The main caveat is that ASD features are usually embedded within a broader syndromic intellectual disability/epilepsy phenotype rather than isolated ASD, and some supporting papers (e.g., array-CGH, PMID 38048114) rest on multigene CNVs, so points are split between Established and Existing.
